Depending on its structure and areas of practice, a Saudi law firm may provide services such as:

  • Corporate and commercial legal advice
  • Company formation and restructuring
  • Contract drafting and review
  • Litigation and court representation
  • Commercial dispute resolution
  • Debt collection and recovery
  • Enforcement of judgments
  • Regulatory and compliance advice
  • Notary and document-related services
  • Inheritance and asset management
  • Support for foreign investors and international businesses

For example, AlKhorayef Law Firm’s current service offering covers litigation and court representation, corporate and commercial advisory, contract documentation, enforcement, debt collection, notary and attestation, asset and inheritance management, and regulatory compliance.

Why AlKhorayef Law Firm May Be Suitable for Certain Clients

AlKhorayef Law Firm is a Riyadh-based Saudi law firm serving individuals, businesses, and international entities operating in the Kingdom. Its website describes a practice built around Saudi legal knowledge, litigation, corporate and commercial advisory, enforcement, debt recovery, inheritance matters, and legal consultancy.

Its suitability depends on the client’s requirements.

For businesses involved in commercial disputes, the firm’s litigation practice covers matters including contract disputes, partnership and shareholder disputes, financial claims, and representation before Saudi courts. Clients can review the firm’s litigation and court representation services when assessing whether this area matches their needs.

For creditors, its debt collection services in Saudi Arabia cover demand notices, negotiation, court representation, and recovery-related procedures.

For matters involving judgment execution, clients can also review the firm’s enforcement services in Saudi Arabia, which focus on enforcing court judgments, recovering debts, contract enforcement, and execution procedures.

For individuals and families, its asset and inheritance management services address estate and inheritance-related legal matters.

This makes the firm potentially relevant when a client needs several connected legal services rather than assistance with only one isolated document.

Choosing a Law Firm for a Business

Businesses should look beyond the immediate legal problem and consider whether the firm can support future requirements.

A company entering Saudi Arabia, for example, may initially need assistance with incorporation and regulatory requirements. Later, it may need contract drafting, employment advice, corporate governance, dispute resolution, debt recovery, or enforcement.

A law firm with relevant corporate and commercial capabilities can provide continuity as the business develops.

For foreign investors, local legal knowledge is especially important. Saudi market-entry requirements can involve multiple authorities and regulatory considerations, making early legal planning valuable. Businesses planning to enter the Kingdom can also review this guide on how to set up a company in Saudi Arabia.

Foreign investors should also understand potential compliance risks before beginning operations. AlKhorayef’s guide to common legal mistakes foreign investors make in Saudi Arabia covers issues such as licensing, contracts, tax compliance, employment requirements, and dispute-resolution planning.

Choosing a Law Firm for Individuals

Individuals should first identify the specific legal issue and then select a lawyer with relevant experience.

For example, inheritance matters require different expertise from commercial litigation. Similarly, a person involved in a contractual dispute may need a lawyer experienced in civil or commercial claims rather than a general legal consultant.

Ask the firm:

  1. Have you handled matters similar to mine?
  2. Who will actually handle my case?
  3. What documents do you need?
  4. What are the major legal risks?
  5. What are the possible stages of the matter?
  6. How will fees be calculated?
  7. How will I receive updates?

Clear answers to these questions can help you make a more informed decision.

Choosing a Law Firm for International Clients

International businesses and foreign investors often need more than knowledge of Saudi law. They may also require communication in English, document coordination, cross-border recovery, regulatory support, or coordination with lawyers in another jurisdiction.

The right firm should be able to explain Saudi requirements clearly to international clients and identify where local legal procedures interact with international transactions.

For cross-border disputes, enforcement can be particularly important. Businesses with foreign judgments or arbitral awards can also review AlKhorayef’s guide on enforcing a foreign court judgment in Saudi Arabia to understand the issues that may arise in cross-border enforcement.

Questions to Ask Before Hiring a Saudi Law Firm

Before formally engaging a firm, ask for clarity on:

  • The lawyer responsible for your matter
  • Relevant experience and practice area
  • Scope of legal services
  • Expected stages of the case
  • Key risks and potential complications
  • Communication arrangements
  • Fee structure
  • Required documentation
  • Whether additional specialists or foreign counsel may be required

Avoid selecting a lawyer solely on price. The cheapest option may not provide the experience or resources required for a complex legal matter.

Final Thoughts

The right law firm in Saudi Arabia is not necessarily the largest firm, the most expensive firm, or the firm described as “the best.” It is the firm whose legal expertise, experience, resources, communication, and approach match your particular needs.

For individuals, businesses, investors, and international clients, the decision should be based on practice-area expertise, Saudi legal knowledge, professional credentials, relevant experience, transparent communication, and the firm’s ability to handle the matter from start to finish.

Before making a decision, compare several suitable options, verify professional credentials, understand the scope of work, and choose legal counsel based on the nature and complexity of your matter.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the top law firms in Saudi Arabia?

There is no single official list that establishes the top law firm in Saudi Arabia for every legal matter. Legal directories such as Legal 500 evaluate firms across specific practice areas, while client requirements vary by industry and case type. The appropriate firm should therefore be selected based on relevant expertise, experience, credentials, and the nature of the legal matter.

What is the best law firm in Saudi Arabia?

There is no universally applicable “best” law firm. A firm that is highly suitable for corporate transactions may not be the best choice for litigation, debt recovery, inheritance, or enforcement. The better approach is to compare firms according to their relevant practice-area experience, Saudi legal expertise, professional credentials, communication, and ability to meet your specific requirements.

How do I choose a law firm in Saudi Arabia?

Start by identifying the type of legal assistance you need. Then compare firms based on relevant experience, practice areas, licensed lawyers, communication, fees, and resources. You can also verify lawyer licensing through Saudi Ministry of Justice services and the Saudi Bar Association’s licensed-lawyer directory.

What legal services do law firms in Saudi Arabia provide?

Depending on the firm, services may include corporate and commercial advice, contracts, litigation, dispute resolution, debt collection, enforcement, regulatory compliance, notary services, inheritance and asset management, and support for foreign investors. Always confirm that the specific firm handles the practice area relevant to your matter.

How much does a lawyer or law firm cost in Saudi Arabia?

Legal fees vary depending on the type, complexity, value, urgency, and duration of the matter. Corporate transactions and complex litigation may require substantially more work than a straightforward consultation or document review. Before engagement, ask the firm to clearly explain the scope of work, fee structure, and any additional costs.

Do I need a Saudi lawyer for legal matters in Saudi Arabia?

For matters requiring representation before Saudi courts, it is important to work with a lawyer who is properly licensed to practise in the Kingdom. The Ministry of Justice provides services for searching licensed lawyers and verifying lawyer-license validity.

title: A Backlash Against Data Centers is Another Challenge to the AI Juggernaut
author: Entrepreneur Mirror
excerpt: There is an unnerving low hum coming from data centers, where tens of thousands of chips perform trillions of operations each second to help drive the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution. These chips fuel the text, photos, and videos produced by advanced AI models’ queries. Their computations, which are essentially the turning on and off of minuscule silicon transistors that comprise a chip, are actually silent. However, as with all computers, practically every watt of the enormous electricity need to run this operation is lost as heat, and the sound you hear is the slow buzz of thousands of fans needed to keep the heat from frying the server racks. Depending on the facility’s size, you may hear the thrum of transformers in substations that channel energy. In the United States, opposition to data centers is particularly visible on the political left. Democratic Senator Bernie Sanders has advocated for a freeze on all new development. “People are looking around worried about how quickly the technology is moving, how little control they have over it, how will data centers impact their community in terms of electric rates and water utilisation,” he said to me. title: Top 10 Inspiring Leaders Transforming Industries
author: Entrepreneur Mirror
excerpt: Leadership today goes beyond business growth, financial results, or professional recognition. It is also about influencing how industries evolve, introducing better ways of working, and inspiring others to think differently. Across sectors and regions, leaders are finding new ways to solve problems, build organisations, create opportunities, and respond to changing market needs. The top 10 inspiring leaders featured in this edition represent different paths to leadership, but each is helping shape the future of their respective industries through their work and ideas. The top 10 inspiring leaders come from varied industries, backgrounds, and parts of the world. Some are building businesses and entering new markets, while others are developing new products, introducing fresh approaches, or challenging established ways of doing things. Their stories are different, yet they share a willingness to take responsibility, make difficult decisions, and keep moving forward when circumstances change. For the top 10 inspiring leaders featured here, success is not simply about reaching a position of influence. It is about using that influence to encourage progress and create meaningful change within their industries. As the global business landscape continues to evolve, the top 10 inspiring leaders featured here offer a closer look at the people helping shape what comes next. Their experiences show that industry transformation can come from many directions, whether through entrepreneurship, innovation, technology, new business models, or a fresh understanding of what customers and communities need. From established sectors to emerging fields, the top 10 inspiring leaders are challenging expectations and contributing to the evolution of the industries they serve. Meet the Leaders Transforming Industries Below are the top 10 inspiring leaders recognised for their vision, leadership, innovative thinking, and contributions to the transformation of their industries. 1. Christina Taft and Luxury for Good: Redefining Elegance Through Purpose Christina Taft is an entrepreneur, innovator, collaborator, marketer, and humanitarian whose work brings together luxury, philanthropy, international relationships, and meaningful social impact. As a multiple founder, she has developed initiatives focused on innovation, leadership, and positive contribution, with a strong interest in turning ideas into action. Her experience across luxury, communications, partnerships, and international markets has shaped a clear belief that success should be measured not only by what is achieved, but also by what is given back. With a background in Luxury Management from the International University of Monaco, Christina has built her work around quality, careful planning, strong relationships, and attention to detail. She understands the expectations of premium markets and the importance of presenting people, brands, and ideas in the right way. Her experience in public and business relations has also helped her work with different audiences and build relationships across international networks. She places discretion over exposure, trust over transactions, and quality over quantity. These principles come together through Luxury for Good, the initiative Christina founded to give luxury a deeper sense of purpose. Drawing inspiration from Monaco and its traditions of refinement and philanthropy, the initiative is built around four values: exclusivity, quality, trust, and kindness. Christina believes that luxury does not need to lose its elegance or exclusivity to have a positive purpose. Instead, it can be used to create meaningful experiences, encourage generosity, support humanitarian work, and bring the right people together around causes that matter. Christina’s interests extend across luxury markets, strategic partnerships, communications, and humanitarian work. She has a particular ability to take an idea and work through the practical steps needed to bring it to life. Her approach involves understanding complex situations, finding opportunities, building the right relationships, and maintaining high standards throughout the process. She has also created Motivationology, a theory centred on motivation, resilience, action, and empowerment, reflecting her belief that people should focus on their strengths and find ways to move forward rather than remain defined by their limitations. A deeply personal influence behind Christina’s philosophy is her mother, Victoria “Vicki” Taft. Remembered for her elegance, warmth, humour, beauty, and generous spirit, Victoria embodied many of the qualities that Christina now carries into her own work. For Christina, her mother showed that elegance was about much more than appearance. It was about how a person treated others, the warmth they brought into a room, and their ability to make people feel welcome and valued. That influence has become an important part of Luxury for Good. Christina’s work places genuine relationships above transactions and meaningful contribution above publicity. Through the initiative, she encourages luxury brands, philanthropists, family offices, and influential individuals to consider how their resources, relationships, and influence can be used for the benefit of others. In doing so, she is also honouring the values she learned from Victoria. Christina Taft’s journey shows how personal values can become the foundation for a wider purpose. Her work brings together ambition and ethics, commercial understanding and humanitarian values, elegance and kindness. Rather than treating these qualities as separate, she sees them as parts of the same approach to leadership and success. Through Luxury for Good, Christina is offering a thoughtful view of what luxury can mean today. For her, its greatest value is not simply in what someone owns or experiences, but in what they can contribute. Guided by her mother’s example and her own experience across luxury, business, and international relationships, Christina continues to build a vision where quality is accompanied by kindness, influence is used responsibly, and success has a positive effect on the people around it. 2. George Winstone | Building a More Accessible Future for Textile Recycling

A piece of clothing does not have to end its journey when it leaves someone’s wardrobe. It can be collected, sorted, reused, recycled, and given a purpose beyond its first life. Making that second journey possible, however, requires more than awareness. It requires the right networks, partnerships, and systems to make recycling easy and accessible.

This is where George Winstone brings his experience into focus. With a professional background spanning corporate insurance, investments, alternative sectors, sales, and business development, George has built his career around relationships and commercial networks. Today, as Head of Distribution at Yalla Textiles, he is using that experience to help expand textile recycling across Dubai.

 

His work centres on developing strategic partnerships, increasing clothing-bank placements, strengthening commercial relationships, and creating efficient distribution channels. The aim is simple but ambitious: make it easier for businesses, communities, retailers, schools, organisations, and individuals to participate in textile recycling.

The clothing banks already provide a practical example of this approach. Yalla Textiles collection points have been placed in different community settings, including Atlantis, Club Padel Dubai, and a local mosque. By bringing collection points closer to where people live, work, visit, and spend their time, the process of donating unwanted textiles becomes a more natural part of everyday life.

Yalla Textiles is a Dubai-based textile recycling company focused on collecting, sorting, reusing, and recycling unwanted clothing, while creating wider environmental and community impact. For George, expanding this work means building a network that can operate efficiently and sustainably at scale.

LinkedIn | Website | Email: george@yallatextiles.com 

3. Mohammad Seri Al Refai | Building Operations That Grow With the Business

“Strong operations are built on people, discipline, and the ability to keep moving as the business grows.”

For Mohammad Seri Al Refai, this is more than a business principle. It reflects the way he approached one of the most important responsibilities of his career: managing costs without losing the people an organisation depends on.

With more than 35 years of experience across facility management, waste management, human resources, and large-scale operations in the UAE, Mohammad has spent much of his career working at the point where people, budgets, and business performance meet. His experience has taught him that improving a company’s financial position does not necessarily require reducing its workforce.

His approach became particularly clear during his time at Al Bahiya Facilities and Services, where he served as Senior Operations Manager and Acting Executive Manager.

Rather than responding to cost pressures by terminating employees or reducing salaries, Mohammad looked at the cost structure itself. One of the measures he implemented was the hiring of Emirati employees, which reduced employment visa costs by approximately AED 2,000 per visa. According to Mohammad, this approach generated savings of more than AED 1 million annually in HR costs, while allowing the organisation to retain its existing workforce.

The result went beyond the financial savings. His approach contributed to Al Bahiya achieving Ministry of Labour Category A classification and recognition among the Top 10 employers for Emirati hiring under MOH. Mohammad was also featured on Ajman TV in connection with these achievements.

For him, the experience demonstrated an important point about leadership: solving a cost problem requires understanding where the cost actually comes from.

That way of thinking has followed Mohammad throughout his career. At Abu Dhabi International Cleaning Services (ADICS), where he served as General Manager and Operations Director from 2009 to 2018, he helped grow the workforce from two labourers to 840 while overseeing operations across catering, cleaning, landscaping, and waste management. His responsibilities included P&L management, cost control, contract negotiations, and operational planning.

At Comfort Pro Facility Management, where he has served as Operations Director since 2021, his responsibilities include managing service delivery, client requirements, workforce development, cost management, and business continuity across multiple locations.

Across these roles, Mohammad’s contribution has not simply been about managing larger teams or contracts. It has been about finding practical ways to make organisations work better.

His message to decision-makers is straightforward: cost reduction should not automatically come at the expense of employees. Sometimes, the better answer is to examine the structure, identify the unnecessary costs, and find an approach that improves the business without weakening the workforce.

That philosophy has become one of the defining lessons of Mohammad’s career: good leadership is not only about reducing expenditure. It is about finding smarter ways to create value.

LinkedIn

4. Prof. Dr. Christian Heinrich | Making Carbon Management Smarter

“Moving industry towards net-zero requires not only ambition, but smarter and more efficient ways of managing carbon.”

Prof. Dr. Christian Heinrich is the Co-Founder and Managing Director of carbmee, a company focused on helping industry move towards net-zero through smarter and more efficient carbon management.

His work sits at the intersection of supply chain management, digital innovation, and sustainability. At carbmee, he is part of the team working to provide businesses with solutions for managing carbon emissions and making the path towards lower emissions more practical.

Christian’s academic background is rooted in supply chain management. He holds a PhD in Supply Chain Management, which he completed in cooperation with BASF. This foundation has shaped his understanding of how businesses can approach complex supply chain challenges while adapting to changing demands.

Before co-founding carbmee, Christian worked in consulting, where he was involved in Digital Innovation and Accelerator projects. He also gained experience with S&OP and supply chain software and process roll-outs across different industries. These experiences gave him exposure to both the strategic and practical sides of improving business processes.

That combination of supply chain knowledge and experience with digital transformation has become an important part of his work at carbmee. Rather than treating carbon management as a separate concern, his work focuses on helping industry approach emissions management in a more structured and efficient way.

Today, through carbmee, Christian Heinrich continues to work towards a more practical approach to carbon emission management, bringing together his experience in supply chains, consulting, and digital innovation with the broader goal of supporting industry on its journey towards net-zero.

LinkedIn | Website 

5. Alexandros Kapetanakis | Connecting Defence Expertise with Opportunity

“Innovation matters when it can move from an idea into something that works.”

With more than 30 years of experience across military equipment, technology, defence operations, and international cooperation, Alexandros Kapetanakis has built a career around solving complex technical challenges and bringing organisations together. His experience includes senior roles with the Hellenic Ministry of National Defence, the Hellenic Army, the European Defence Agency, and NATO-related programmes.

Today, Alexandros is the Founder and CEO of EBS Consulting, an Athens-based advisory firm established in 2023. The company supports defence and technology organisations with regulatory requirements, international partnerships, funding opportunities, innovation programmes, and market access across Europe and the NATO ecosystem.

Alexandros holds an Integrated Master’s degree in Electrical and Computer Engineering from NTUA, an MBA, and an MSc in Technology Management. His career has included technical, operational, management, and international cooperation roles within the Greek defence sector.

As Hellenic National Coordinator within the Ministry of National Defence, he worked on industrial security certification and European defence programmes. He also held responsibilities involving international defence cooperation, procurement, weapon-system support, and relations with the European Defence Agency and NATO.

That experience became the foundation for EBS Consulting, where he now applies his understanding of the defence sector to help organisations navigate an increasingly complex European and international market.

EBS Consulting works across areas including security clearances, EU and NATO funding, defence innovation, international collaboration, procurement, and technology development.

The company has supported projects including Raymetrics SA’s successful NATO DIANA Accelerator proposal and Elval-Halcor’s participation in a European Defence Agency workshop on the European Combat Vessel initiative.

Alexandros also brings a strong technical perspective to emerging areas such as AI, sensors, robotics, autonomy, and cybersecurity, helping organisations understand where their capabilities can fit within the wider defence innovation landscape.

Today, his work through EBS Consulting is focused on one clear goal: helping defence and technology organisations turn their capabilities into practical opportunities for innovation, collaboration, and growth.

LinkedIn | Website 

6. Philip Weiser | Four Decades of Building Trust in Luxury Real Estate

“Luxury is not simply about owning an exceptional property. It is about the lifestyle, heritage, and lasting value that come with it.“

For Philip, adapting to change does not mean abandoning the principles that built a business. It means finding new ways to deliver the same level of trust and service in an evolving market.

That balance between experience and innovation continues to shape Carlton International today. The 30-year renown of Carlton International has incited Philp to share the brand with select real estate companies, intent on increasing their visibility and their prestige around the world, so after more than 40 years in the industry, Philip Weiser’s story is not simply one of building a luxury real estate business. It is about developing long-term relationships, understanding the value attached to exceptional properties, and creating a brand capable of evolving without losing sight of what made it successful in the first place.

Today, Carlton International has established itself as a prominent name in luxury real estate on the Côte d’Azur, working across the region from the Italian frontier through Monaco, Cannes, and Saint-Tropez. Its services extend across property sales, prestigious villa rentals, investment advisory, property development, and asset management.

Over the course of more than four decades, Philip has worked with private clients, family offices, developers, and international investors on high-value acquisitions and strategic investments. Yet, for him, the relationship has always mattered as much as the transaction. Discretion, integrity, attention to detail, and personalised advice form the basis of the approach he has brought to Carlton International.

That philosophy has also shaped the wider Carlton Group. Under Philip’s leadership, the group has expanded to include Carlton Signature and Visua Concepts, bringing together luxury property brokerage, asset management, strategic marketing, and international brand licensing.

The luxury property market itself has changed considerably since Philip first entered the industry. Carlton International has responded by embracing new tools and approaches, including artificial intelligence, advanced digital marketing, and international brand licensing. At the same time, the company has remained committed to the personal service that has been central to its identity from the beginning.

For Philip, adapting to change does not mean abandoning the principles that built a business. It means finding new ways to deliver the same level of trust and service in an evolving market.

That balance between experience and innovation continues to shape Carlton International today. After more than 40 years in the industry, Philip Weiser’s story is not simply one of building a luxury real estate business. It is about developing long-term relationships, understanding the value attached to exceptional properties, and creating a brand capable of evolving without losing sight of what made it successful in the first place.

7. Samdavid Jeyaraj | Turning AI Strategy into Real Business Value

“Think deeply. Build practically. Scale responsibly.”

AI is moving quickly into everyday business, but Samdavid Jeyaraj is focused on a more practical question: how can companies make AI genuinely useful? His work is about taking AI beyond experiments and finding ways for it to solve real business problems, improve everyday work, and create measurable value.

As an AI Transformation Leader, Enterprise AI Strategist, Agentic AI Practitioner, Researcher, Author, and Speaker, Samdavid currently works for Landmark Global – specializing in cross-border logistics, a bnode company. Working in an international logistics environment gives him a practical setting to explore how AI can be applied to real operational challenges. His work covers the journey from identifying a problem and developing an AI strategy to testing solutions, putting them into practice, and helping teams use them effectively.

One of the things that sets Samdavid’s approach apart is his focus on connecting ideas with actual business needs. He works with business, technology, data, security, and operations teams to understand problems and find practical ways AI can help. As he puts it, AI success isn’t about how much you build; it’s about how much friction you remove. This practical mindset guides how he evaluates AI opportunities, with the focus staying on solving problems rather than building technology for its own sake.

His work includes generative AI, Agentic AI, document processing, customs and product classification, forecasting, customer service, pricing, sales, and software development.

The goal behind these projects is simple: AI should make a difference. His work has focused on reducing manual work, improving decisions, strengthening compliance, increasing efficiency, and creating potential annual operational value worth hundreds of thousands of euros.

For Samdavid, however, individual AI projects are only the beginning. He sees a bigger opportunity in creating workplaces where AI tools, AI agents, company knowledge, and human expertise can work together.

Why Agentic AI Matters

A major area of Samdavid’s work today is Agentic AI.

He believes businesses will move beyond using AI simply as chatbots or assistants. Instead, AI agents could increasingly handle tasks such as finding information, working through problems, coordinating activities, and carrying out parts of a workflow.

But he does not believe that giving AI more control is enough.

His approach involves using different AI models and agents for different jobs, rather than depending on one technology. At the same time, people with real knowledge of logistics, customs, finance, pricing, and operations remain important in checking and improving how these AI systems work.

The idea is straightforward: AI can handle scale, people bring judgment, and clear rules help keep the process trustworthy.

Trust Has to Be Built In

Samdavid also believes that companies need to think about safety and trust from the beginning when building AI systems.

Privacy, security, data access, choosing the right model, checking results, and keeping people involved are all part of the process. These considerations should not be added only after an AI system has already been built.

For him, successful AI is not simply about whether a system works. It also needs to be secure, understandable, measurable, and trusted by the people using it.

Looking at the Human Side of AI

Alongside his professional work, Samdavid is pursuing doctoral-level business research on Agentic AI adoption and organisational productivity in logistics.

His research looks at a question that will become increasingly important as AI enters everyday work: what makes people trust AI enough to actually use it?

He is studying the relationship between Agentic AI adoption, trust in AI, AI governance, and organisational productivity. His professional experience gives him the opportunity to build and work with AI systems, while his research allows him to look more closely at the people and organisations using them.

Samdavid is also developing his ideas through writing and speaking. His work explores what happens when AI begins taking on parts of knowledge-based work and how people and AI systems can work together.

His speaking topics include building the Agentic Enterprise, Human + Agent Operating Models, Multi-Model AI Strategy, AI Governance, and moving from AI experiments to real business value.

Rather than focusing only on what AI might be able to do one day, Samdavid’s work asks a more practical question: what should businesses be doing today to prepare for it?

For Samdavid, the answer is not the number of AI models a company has built or the number of experiments it has completed.

Better decisions. Better customer experiences. Better productivity. Better business results.

That is the kind of AI transformation Samdavid Jeyaraj is working towards: technology that is not just impressive, but genuinely useful.

LinkedIn | Website

8. Jay P. Patel | Turning Quality, Technology and Leadership into Results

“Excellence is not only about improving systems. It is about helping people and organisations become better at what they do.”

With more than 30 years of leadership experience, Jay P. Patel has built a career around helping organisations improve how they work, make decisions, and prepare for change. His experience spans manufacturing, healthcare, professional services, technology, and enterprise transformation, with a particular focus on AI strategy, operational excellence, quality, and governance.

Jay is the Founder, CEO and President of Quality & Productivity Solutions, Inc., a consulting and advisory firm he founded in 1996. The company works across more than 15 countries, supporting organisations with AI strategy, digital transformation, Lean Six Sigma, quality systems, and performance improvement. Over the years, Jay has designed and led more than 200 courses and initiatives covering AI, quality, leadership, and organisational transformation.

His career began in engineering and manufacturing, including roles with General Electric, Bendix-AlliedSignal, Carrier Corporation, and Cabot Safety Corporation. These positions gave him a strong foundation in engineering, manufacturing operations, quality management, and process improvement before he moved further into consulting and executive advisory work.

Today, his work increasingly brings together technology and business strategy. Jay advises senior leaders on AI adoption, digital transformation, risk, quality, and organisational performance, with an emphasis on making new technology useful rather than simply adopting it for the sake of change.

His experience also extends to governance. Since 2024, Jay has served as a Board Trustee of Bhagyoday Charity Trust – Healthcare & Medical College, where he contributes to discussions around institutional strategy, healthcare quality, risk management, regulatory compliance, and long-term sustainability.

Alongside his consulting and board work, Jay has remained active in professional organisations. He serves in leadership roles within the American Society for Quality (ASQ), the Institute of Industrial Engineers, and the Project Management Institute. He is also an ASQ Fellow and recipient of the Lancaster Medal, recognising his contribution to quality excellence.

His academic and professional background includes a Master’s degree in Electrical Engineering, an MBA, a Master Lean Six Sigma Black Belt, PMP and Scrum Master credentials, and more than 30 professional certifications and certificates across areas including AI, quality, digital transformation, and leadership. He is also the author of 12 published books, with additional books currently in process.

What ties Jay’s work together is his belief that transformation should benefit both the organisation and the people within it. Technology, processes, and systems can improve performance, but lasting results depend on capable leaders, strong teams, and a culture that can sustain those improvements.

After more than three decades in the field, Jay continues to work at that intersection, helping organisations approach AI, quality, leadership, and transformation with a practical focus on long-term performance rather than short-term change.

LinkedIn | Website

9. Nele De Smet | Building a Business Around Beauty, Purpose and People

“For me, being an entrepreneur is about creation.”

Nele De Smet is a second-generation family business owner, CEO, and mother of three sons. Her professional journey has taken her through different experiences before bringing her to Evolta, an engineering and architecture company with 125 professionals. Founded by her father, the company eventually became the place where she chose to take on a new challenge and build her own path as a leader.

In 2020, at the beginning of the COVID-19 crisis, Nele completed a family buyout and took full ownership of the company. It was a decision rooted not only in business, but in how strongly she believes in the work Evolta does. Her ambition is to build an organisation that makes a difference, both through the spaces it creates and through the way it contributes to a more sustainable world.

For Nele, the work is ultimately about people. She speaks about the happiness that can come from creating spaces where people feel at home, while also thinking about the wider responsibility that comes with designing and building for the long term. Her goal is to build on Evolta’s position in Belgium and eventually become a top 30 player in the European market.

Sustainability has become an important part of that direction. Nele recalibrated the company’s focus and defined its mission as “contributing to a beautiful world in balance, to happy people in development and to a sustainable organisation on the move.” She describes Evolta’s values as entrepreneurial, inventive, candid, and resilient, with resilience being particularly important to her understanding of sustainability.

Her own path into leadership was not conventional. At 18, Nele chose to study political and social sciences at the University of Ghent, majoring in communication. Alongside her university studies, she completed an evening course in journalism in Brussels and graduated with distinction in 1999. She later earned an MBA from Vlerick Leuven Gent Management School in 2000 and became an MIT alumnus in 2025, holding a degree as Chief Sustainability Officer. She has also received the Fire Hydrant Award.

But Nele is clear that a career is not built on qualifications and ambition alone. Nothing meaningful comes easy. Her journey has included doubt, difficult periods, uncertainty, and moments when taking the next step required courage. For her, the answer has been to continue, even when she was afraid.

Her own experience has taught her that courage is not about having no fear. It is about being willing to take the risk anyway. “Choose love, not fear” is one of the principles she lives by, alongside another simple reminder: “Be afraid and do it anyway.”

Going all in, working hard, adapting when circumstances change, and finding strength within herself have all played a part in her journey. She believes people often discover what they are capable of only when they test their boundaries and challenge their limits.

She also places great value on the people who stay. The people who stand beside you during difficult periods, rather than only appearing when everything is going well, become an important part of the journey. For Nele, success is not only about what you build, but also about who you build it with and who remains beside you along the way.

Behind the titles and achievements is a much more personal idea of leadership. Nele describes her vision simply: to create beauty and live fully. She sees beauty as something deeply personal, shaped by the person looking at it. Different perspectives, she believes, do not diminish beauty; they add to it.

That perspective reaches back to her childhood, when she says she looked at the world with wonder and found beauty in unexpected people and places. Today, she wants to carry that same sense of wonder into her work and her relationships, creating beauty wherever she goes and making the people she meets feel special.

Her understanding of life has also been shaped by loss. Saying goodbye to people she wanted to keep close taught her about the scarcity of time and the value of each moment. It strengthened her belief that what ultimately matters is how we touch other people’s lives and allow them to touch ours.

This is where her philosophy of “Panta Rhei”, meaning everything flows, becomes particularly important. For Nele, life and business are not meant to remain fixed. Things change, people change, and circumstances change. The challenge is to move with that change, rather than resist it.

She believes we should find our own state of flow and, just as importantly, find the people and places where we can grow and flow.

That philosophy is perhaps the clearest thread connecting Nele’s personal and professional life. She wants to create, to build, to make space for others, but also to encourage people to live in a way that feels genuinely their own. Her journey has shown her that growth requires both openness and courage: the willingness to change direction, challenge yourself, and keep going when things become difficult.

“Breathe. Love. Laugh. Dance. Rest. Strive. Stumble. Cry. Embrace. Break. Heal. Flow. Go. Roar. Mess it up. Try again. Be grateful and enjoy every piece of it.”

For Nele De Smet, building a company and building a life are not separate things. Both are about creation, beauty, resilience, courage, and making the most of the time we are given.

LinkedIn | Website

10. Ali Almakrami | Engineering, Leadership, and the Drive to Create Meaningful Impact

Engineering is often associated with equations, technical knowledge, and problem-solving. For Ali Almakrami, an Electrical Engineering student at Najran University, it is also about people, leadership, and finding ways to turn ideas into meaningful outcomes.

Throughout his university journey, Ali has actively pursued opportunities that combine technical development with collaboration and service. He is the Founder of the Engineering Club, where he helped establish a platform that encourages engineering students to collaborate, develop their skills, and take part in meaningful activities and initiatives.

His interest in supporting others has also shaped his experience as a Peer Mentor. In this role, Ali supported fellow students throughout their academic journey while helping foster a more collaborative and supportive learning environment. For him, leadership is not simply about holding a position. It is about creating opportunities for others to grow.

That approach has continued through his involvement with IEEE and the College of Engineering. Ali previously served as Vice President of the IEEE Student Branch at Najran University and as Vice President of the Student Advisory Council at the College of Engineering. These experiences strengthened his skills in strategic planning, teamwork, communication, organization, and decision-making.

Today, he serves as General Advisor of the IEEE Student Branch, where he continues to contribute by providing guidance, sharing his experience, supporting leadership development, and helping the team work towards sustainable growth and impactful initiatives.

While leadership has become an important part of Ali’s university experience, his focus remains connected to engineering. He continues to develop his capabilities in critical thinking, analytical problem-solving, creativity, innovation, adaptability, resilience, and strategic thinking.

Ali believes that becoming a successful engineer requires more than technical knowledge. The ability to communicate, collaborate, adapt to challenges, and make thoughtful decisions is equally important when turning technical knowledge into meaningful solutions.

This belief has encouraged him to look beyond the classroom and seek experiences that challenge him to take responsibility, work with others, and contribute to the wider academic community.

As Ali continues his studies at Najran University, he remains eager to learn, take on new challenges, and explore opportunities where engineering, innovation, and leadership come together.

His journey so far reflects his belief that meaningful impact comes from combining knowledge with initiative and collaboration. For Ali, becoming a successful engineer means being prepared to lead, solve complex problems, adapt to change, and turn ideas into solutions that matter.

It is this combination of engineering and leadership that continues to shape the professional he hopes to become.

LinkedIn | Website

Conclusion

The top 10 inspiring leaders featured in this list demonstrate that transforming an industry requires more than achievement alone. Their journeys reflect the value of vision, persistence, innovation, and the willingness to approach familiar challenges in new ways. While their industries and experiences may differ, the top 10 inspiring leaders share an ability to turn ideas into action and encourage progress within the organizations and sectors they influence.

Their stories also show that industry transformation is an ongoing process. The top 10 inspiring leaders continue to adapt, learn, and explore new possibilities as markets, technologies, and expectations change. By questioning established practices and pursuing better ways forward, they are helping shape the future of their industries and inspiring others to do the same.

title: Compensation And Air Traffic Chaos: Shutdown Cost us More than £1,000
author: Entrepreneur Mirror
excerpt: It should have been Catie and Phil Allen’s first vacation in two and a half years. Rather, they are at home begging for unpaid refunds. The four-hour closure of the UK’s air traffic control system on Tuesday confused thousands of travellers, including the couple. This suggests their trip to Slovenia has been cancelled, and although British Airways reimbursed them for their travel, they expect to pay £1,300 out of pocket for unused lodging and activities. After issues at UK airports, it’s not the first time and it won’t be the last—that travellers are left on a wing and a prayer. Here’s how their situation connects to others and the reasons behind their severe setback. aboard Tuesday, Catie, 30, and Phil, 34, were seated aboard a British Airways flight to Ljubljana that never got off. Airlines are required to send passengers to their destination as soon as feasible at no additional expense in the event of a flight cancellation, even if it is with a competitor airline. Alternatively, travellers can request a refund, which should be provided for flights delayed by more than five hours. title: Matthew Leesbourne | Building Businesses That Put People First
author: Entrepreneur Mirror
excerpt: For Matthew Leesbourne, a career that began at 17 as a bellman grew into a broader focus on hospitality, leadership, technology, and human behaviour. Today, through Layker & Leesbourne, he brings these areas together across hospitality, AI, food innovation, entertainment, publishing, and social impact. We spoke with Matthew Leesbourne about how his work has evolved, the role of technology in business, and his belief that organisations can create both commercial value and meaningful opportunities for people. The Journey Behind the Work We began by asking Matthew about the experiences that shaped his approach to business and leadership. “How did your early career in hospitality shape the way you approach business and leadership today?” He explained that his professional journey began in hospitality at the operational level as a bellman at the age of 17, before progressing through Front Office, Guest Relations, Rooms Division, Quality Assurance, Learning & Development and Strategic Leadership. “Working from the ground up gave me an important perspective that continues to influence how I lead today: regardless of how sophisticated an organisation becomes, every commercial outcome ultimately involves people. Throughout my career, I became increasingly interested in the relationship between human behaviour, guest experience, employee performance, operational efficiency and commercial results. Rather than simply asking what happened, I wanted to understand why it happened, what behaviours contributed to it, and whether those patterns could be identified early enough to influence the eventual outcome. That thinking gradually expanded beyond traditional hospitality. Today, through Layker & Leesbourne, our work encompasses an interconnected ecosystem across hospitality, behavioural intelligence and artificial intelligence, food innovation, entertainment and experiences, publishing, human development and social-impact initiatives. Ultimately, whether we are developing a hotel experience, technology platform, consumer product, entertainment concept or social initiative, the fundamental question remains remarkably similar: How can we understand people better and use that understanding to create something of sustainable value?” From Individual Businesses to an Ecosystem We then asked Matthew how his work has evolved from individual businesses and projects into a broader ecosystem. “How has your work evolved over the years, and what led you towards building an interconnected ecosystem rather than focusing on one industry?” Matthew Leesbourne explained that the biggest change has been moving away from individual businesses and projects towards an interconnected ecosystem. “Initially, many of our ideas addressed specific opportunities within particular industries. Hospitality addressed guest experiences and operations. Technology addressed intelligence and efficiency. Food innovation addressed consumer markets. Entertainment created experiences and connections. Publishing explored human experiences, leadership and personal development. Eventually, we recognised that these areas were not as disconnected as conventional corporate structures might suggest. That became an important part of the philosophy behind Layker & Leesbourne. Rather than simply creating a portfolio of unrelated companies, we are developing an ecosystem in which knowledge, technology, intellectual property, talent, relationships and capabilities can move between enterprises. Our evolution has therefore been from asking, ‘How do we build successful businesses?’ to ‘How do we build an ecosystem where successful businesses strengthen one another while creating sustainable economic and human impact?’” Creating Value Beyond the Business We next asked Matthew Leesbourne how he sees his work contributing beyond commercial success. “How do you think businesses can create commercial value while also contributing to the wider community and creating meaningful opportunities for people?” He said the focus is on connecting commercial development with human capability, innovation and social impact. “We do not believe businesses should simply extract economic value from the environments in which they operate. Wherever possible, they should return something: knowledge, employment, capability, opportunity, innovation and social value. Through InterventioNow, our philanthropic division, we focus on employability, workforce readiness, skills development, training and reintegration. We want to move beyond simply telling people that they deserve another opportunity. Where possible, we want to help create the structure that makes that opportunity sustainable. For us, sustainable impact means creating an ecosystem in which businesses perform commercially, employees progress professionally, customers receive meaningful experiences, partners grow alongside us and communities benefit from the economic activities surrounding those enterprises.” Matthew Leesbourne on What Makes a Strong Leader Today? Turning to leadership, we asked Matthew Leesbourne which qualities he believes matter most in today’s business environment. “What three qualities do you believe are most important for leaders trying to succeed in today’s rapidly changing business environment?” He identified three qualities that have remained important throughout his own experience. “I would identify adaptability, emotional intelligence and analytical curiosity. Industries no longer evolve independently. Technology, consumer behaviour, economic conditions, geopolitical developments and social expectations can transform an operating environment remarkably quickly. Leaders must therefore be prepared to challenge established ways of working. Emotional intelligence is equally important because whether you are operating a hotel, developing technology, managing employees, negotiating with partners or building a consumer brand, ultimately you are dealing with human behaviour. The third is analytical curiosity. Businesses today possess extraordinary amounts of data. The competitive advantage is no longer simply having information. It is knowing what questions to ask of that information. Data tells us what is happening. Human observation and behavioural understanding help us understand why.” Technology Should Solve a Real Problem We then turned to artificial intelligence and asked Matthew Leesbourne how he believes businesses should approach the rapid development of new technology. “How do you think businesses should approach AI, and what role should technology play in the future of business?” He believes the opportunity is significant, but technology should always begin with a clear purpose. “Technology should never be implemented simply because it is fashionable. The first question should always be: ‘What problem are we solving?’ Artificial intelligence can process enormous volumes of information, identify patterns and support decision-making at a scale that would be impossible for an individual. But human beings still provide judgement, empathy, creativity, context and emotional connection. The most powerful organisations will therefore not necessarily be those with the most technology. They will be those that understand how to combine machine intelligence with human intelligence. Technology should provide intelligence.

That became an important part of the philosophy behind Layker & Leesbourne. Rather than simply creating a portfolio of unrelated companies, we are developing an ecosystem in which knowledge, technology, intellectual property, talent, relationships and capabilities can move between enterprises.

Our evolution has therefore been from asking, ‘How do we build successful businesses?’ to ‘How do we build an ecosystem where successful businesses strengthen one another while creating sustainable economic and human impact?’”

Creating Value Beyond the Business

We next asked Matthew Leesbourne how he sees his work contributing beyond commercial success.

“How do you think businesses can create commercial value while also contributing to the wider community and creating meaningful opportunities for people?”

He said the focus is on connecting commercial development with human capability, innovation and social impact.

“We do not believe businesses should simply extract economic value from the environments in which they operate. Wherever possible, they should return something: knowledge, employment, capability, opportunity, innovation and social value.

Through InterventioNow, our philanthropic division, we focus on employability, workforce readiness, skills development, training and reintegration. We want to move beyond simply telling people that they deserve another opportunity. Where possible, we want to help create the structure that makes that opportunity sustainable.

For us, sustainable impact means creating an ecosystem in which businesses perform commercially, employees progress professionally, customers receive meaningful experiences, partners grow alongside us and communities benefit from the economic activities surrounding those enterprises.”

Matthew Leesbourne on What Makes a Strong Leader Today?

Turning to leadership, we asked Matthew Leesbourne which qualities he believes matter most in today’s business environment.

“What three qualities do you believe are most important for leaders trying to succeed in today’s rapidly changing business environment?”

He identified three qualities that have remained important throughout his own experience.

“I would identify adaptability, emotional intelligence and analytical curiosity.

Industries no longer evolve independently. Technology, consumer behaviour, economic conditions, geopolitical developments and social expectations can transform an operating environment remarkably quickly. Leaders must therefore be prepared to challenge established ways of working.

Emotional intelligence is equally important because whether you are operating a hotel, developing technology, managing employees, negotiating with partners or building a consumer brand, ultimately you are dealing with human behaviour.

The third is analytical curiosity. Businesses today possess extraordinary amounts of data. The competitive advantage is no longer simply having information. It is knowing what questions to ask of that information.

Data tells us what is happening. Human observation and behavioural understanding help us understand why.”

Technology Should Solve a Real Problem

We then turned to artificial intelligence and asked Matthew Leesbourne how he believes businesses should approach the rapid development of new technology.

“How do you think businesses should approach AI, and what role should technology play in the future of business?”

He believes the opportunity is significant, but technology should always begin with a clear purpose.

“Technology should never be implemented simply because it is fashionable. The first question should always be: ‘What problem are we solving?’

Artificial intelligence can process enormous volumes of information, identify patterns and support decision-making at a scale that would be impossible for an individual. But human beings still provide judgement, empathy, creativity, context and emotional connection.

The most powerful organisations will therefore not necessarily be those with the most technology. They will be those that understand how to combine machine intelligence with human intelligence.

Technology should provide intelligence. People should provide meaning.”

Creating Opportunities for Second Beginnings

Finally, we asked Matthew Leesbourne about the role businesses can play in helping people overcome difficult circumstances and build a new professional future.

“What can businesses do to create meaningful opportunities for people whose personal circumstances or past experiences may have made their professional journey more difficult?”

Matthew Leesbourne spoke about the importance of looking beyond a person’s past and recognising what they are capable of becoming.

“A person’s past should not automatically determine the opportunities available in their future.

Whether someone comes from a disadvantaged family environment, has experienced incarceration or substance dependency, survived abuse, or simply lived outside what society considers a conventional pathway, our first question is not, ‘What happened to you?’ It is, ‘Who are you today, what are you genuinely capable of, and what can we build from here?’

We do not believe in creating opportunities purely from sympathy. We believe in creating opportunities based on potential, capability, accountability and the willingness to progress.

Businesses have the capacity to create more than employment. They can create second beginnings.

If an individual possesses the capability, commitment and genuine willingness to move forward, their background should provide context to their story, not become the permanent definition of their future. For us, opportunity begins by seeing the person first.”

Conclusion

Matthew’s approach ultimately brings his commercial and social thinking together. Whether the work involves hospitality, technology, food, entertainment, publishing or workforce development, the underlying question remains the same: how can businesses create value while also creating opportunities for people?

His answer is captured in the philosophy behind Layker & Leesbourne: “Purpose Beyond Profit. Innovation Beyond Industries. Humanity Beyond Generations.”

Didin Nasirudin, Co-Founder and Managing Director of Bening Communication, has built a career that has moved across several different worlds. His journey began with nuclear engineering, followed by management, journalism, and eventually public relations. Over the years, these experiences have shaped a broader approach to communications, one that combines business understanding, media knowledge, stakeholder relations, political communication, and geopolitical insight.

Today, his work goes beyond traditional public relations. Through Bening Communication, Didin works with organisations on strategic communications, reputation, government and stakeholder relations, crisis and issue management, and digital communications. His doctoral studies in political communications and diplomacy have also brought him into contact with government officials, parliament members, political activists, academics, researchers, and policy practitioners.

We spoke with Didin about his unconventional career, the evolution of Bening Communication, the changing role of technology, and why communication today requires a much wider view of the world.

A Career That Took an Unexpected Turn

We began by looking at the path that brought Didin into communications, which was far removed from where he initially expected his career to go.

“Could you start by telling us about your journey and work?”

Looking back, Didin sees the different stages of his career as connected rather than unrelated. Each one gave him a different way of understanding complex situations and communicating with different audiences.

“My professional journey has been quite unconventional. I graduated in Nuclear Engineering from Gadjah Mada University because, from a young age, I was fascinated by science, atoms, nuclear technology, and quantum physics. My original ambition was to work at a nuclear power plant that the Indonesian government was planning to develop. When that project did not materialize, I had to rethink my future and move into the private sector.”

He began as a management trainee at Sinar Mas Group and later Tigaraksa Group before the 1997–1998 Asian financial crisis changed the direction of his early career.

“At different points, I worked as a lecturer and managed a branch of an English-language course, and became a journalist. Eventually, at the end of 1999, I entered public relations.”

That move eventually led to Bening Communication, where he has been a co-founder and Managing Director since 2008. For Didin, his engineering background, journalism experience, and years in PR have each added something different to the way he works today.

“Nuclear engineering taught me structured thinking and how to simplify complex issues. Journalism taught me how the media works and how to identify what makes a story relevant. Public relations taught me how organizations build trust, manage perceptions, communicate strategically, and engage multiple stakeholders whose interests do not always align.”

How Bening Communication Has Changed

We then turned to Bening Communication and how the company has changed as the communications industry itself has evolved.

“How has your company/work evolved since you started?”

Didin explained that the company has always tried to remain flexible rather than relying on one fixed way of working.

“I have always described Bening as a malleable organization. By that I mean we should never assume that the way we operate today will necessarily be the way we operate tomorrow.”

Bening initially developed a particularly strong reputation in technology PR and has worked with more than 150 local and international brands. Over time, its work has expanded into a much broader range of communications services.

“Today, we combine Traditional PR with Content Development, Event Management, Strategic Media Collaborations, Digital Marketing, Social Media Management, KOL and Influencer Engagement, Community Engagement, Government Relations, and Crisis and Issue Management.”

The company has also placed greater emphasis on data, monitoring, and research, including real-time news and social media monitoring, newsroom analysis, SEO, and GEO.

For Didin, this reflects a wider change in what businesses now expect from communications.

“So Bening’s evolution has not simply been about adding more services. It has been about moving from media relations to integrated reputation management, public affairs, strategic intelligence, and executive-level counsel.”

Communication as Part of the Wider Business Picture

We next explored how Didin sees Bening’s role within the wider business and communications ecosystem in Indonesia.

“How does your work contribute to the ecosystem in your region?”

For him, communication has an economic role because businesses need trust and credibility to build lasting relationships with their stakeholders.

“The first contribution is building trust between organizations and their stakeholders. A company may have an excellent product, technology, or business model, but if it cannot clearly explain its value, establish credibility, or respond effectively when problems arise, its ability to grow will be limited.”

That work now extends beyond consumers and journalists. Bening also works around communities, government, regulators, industry associations, and other stakeholders who can influence an organisation’s operating environment.

Didin’s academic work has strengthened this side of his professional life, giving him regular interaction with people across politics, government, academia, and public policy.

“These relationships are not simply contacts; more importantly, they improve my understanding of how different actors think, what concerns them, how they interpret public issues, and how policy debates evolve.”

His interest in U.S. politics and geopolitics adds another dimension. He points out that international developments can quickly become business issues for companies operating in Indonesia through investment, trade, technology, energy, supply chains, and political relationships.

“For C-level executives and investors, communications advice alone may therefore be insufficient. They sometimes need help interpreting the wider environment.”

This has gradually moved his own role towards strategic counsel, where communications are considered alongside political, regulatory, reputational, and geopolitical developments.

Three Qualities That Matter

We then asked Didin what he believes professionals need in order to build lasting careers in a communications industry that is constantly changing.

“What three qualities do you believe are critical for success in your industry?”

His answer came down to three things.

“If I had to choose only three, adaptability, resilience, and trustworthiness.”

He sees adaptability as essential because the communications industry has moved from traditional media relations to online media, social platforms, influencers, data, and now artificial intelligence.

“Adaptability, however, does not mean chasing every trend. It means understanding which changes are structural and which are temporary.”

Resilience, meanwhile, comes from experience. Bening has had to navigate financial crises, client losses, and the COVID-19 pandemic.

“A crisis can force you to become more efficient, more flexible, or more creative.”

The third quality, trustworthiness, becomes particularly important when working closely with executives, investors, journalists, policymakers, and other stakeholders.

“PR, government relations, lobbying, political consulting, and executive counsel all depend on credibility.”

What Technology Is Changing

From there, we turned to technology and the growing role of artificial intelligence in business and communications.

“What are your views on the current technological advancements in the business world?”

Didin’s response is shaped partly by his own background in engineering and his years working with technology companies. He sees AI as a major shift, particularly because of its ability to process information, analyse data, automate repetitive work, and support decision-making.

“Artificial intelligence, in particular, will profoundly change the way businesses operate.”

He also sees the impact directly within communications. Media monitoring, social listening, research, content development, and analysis can all now be supported by AI.

Another change he highlights is the way people discover information. Traditional SEO is increasingly being joined by GEO, or Generative Engine Optimization, as people begin using AI platforms to find information and recommendations.

“For a communications business such as ours, this means technology is no longer simply a tool that supports PR. It is becoming part of the communications environment itself.”

However, Didin does not see AI as a replacement for human judgment.

“My approach is not humans versus AI but humans working with AI.”

He believes technology can help businesses become faster and better informed, while qualities such as trust, empathy, creativity, ethical judgment, leadership, and relationships remain deeply human.

Lessons From an Unconventional Career

Finally, we asked Didin what advice he would give someone trying to establish themselves in the communications industry, particularly given the unexpected turns in his own career.

“How would you guide someone to navigate the key challenges you faced when establishing yourself in this industry?”

His first lesson is that careers do not always follow a straight line.

“The first thing I would tell them is: do not expect a straight career path. Mine certainly was not.”

He encourages people to learn through experience while continuing to develop themselves through education and exposure to different fields.

“Learn by doing, but never stop upgrading yourself.”

He also believes that relationships should be built before they are needed, and that businesses should prepare for difficult periods rather than assuming everything will remain stable.

“Build relationships before you urgently need them.”

Reputation, he says, deserves the same attention as revenue.

“Protect your reputation with the same seriousness you protect your revenue.”

Perhaps his most personal advice is not to allow work to consume everything else.

“No one should die for business.”

For Didin, a long career is not simply about building a company or reaching a particular position. It is about remaining curious, adapting when circumstances change, building meaningful relationships, and being willing to follow opportunities that may not have been part of the original plan.

“My own career shows that the destination can be very different from the original plan. I began by wanting to work in nuclear technology and eventually found myself advising companies, engaging with political and policy stakeholders, studying political communication, and analyzing U.S. politics and geopolitics. Sometimes the unexpected path is exactly where your most distinctive value is created.”

Why Founders Should Stay Uncomfortable

Ask Nils Ehle how he decides which opportunities to pursue, and he won’t talk about market sizing or funding rounds. “You have to refuse to get stuck on the skills and projects you’ve already done,” he says. “AI is the current layer to embrace, and it’s fundamentally a business skill, not a technology topic.”

For Nils Ehle, the engagements worth taking are the ones with a genuine spark in them, a client who wants to build something real rather than simply cut costs. “If you want to stay relevant, you cannot stay in your comfort zone, not as a founder, not as a company,” he says. “Comfort is where reinvention quietly dies.”

Building Core Strength Instead of Chasing Use Cases

Many entrepreneurs building in the AI space fall into the same trap: leading with flashy use cases instead of foundational capability. Nils Ehle sees this constantly in the clients who come to him after a failed pilot. “AI business transformation is not a use-case sport. It’s a capability-building exercise,” he says.

You need a strong back, strong legs, a strong core.”

A Founder’s Take on Leadership

Running a growing practice has sharpened Nils Ehle’s views on what leadership actually requires in an AI-saturated world. He points to an image he returns to often: the elephant, whose heart weighs roughly five times more than its brain, compared to humans, where the ratio is reversed. “Most modern leadership is built on that imbalance, heavy on analysis, light on heart,” he says. “The founders and leaders I see succeeding are the ones who deliberately shift toward heart-based leadership.”

He’s equally direct about vulnerability at the top. “You do not have to have all the answers,” Nils Ehle says. “The leaders I see thriving are willing to stand in front of their teams and say, I don’t know yet, let’s figure this out together.”

Alongside consulting, Nils Ehle has been building AI Use Case Engine with network partners, a real-time system that breaks a company down into its core business capabilities, then proposes and prioritizes AI and automation use cases benchmarked against real-world examples. “We deliberately run it alongside human experience and intuition that AI alone can’t provide,” he says, describing it as pairing narrow artificial intelligence with what he calls general human intuitive intelligence.

Asked what advice shaped his own founder’s path, Nils Ehle doesn’t reach for a productivity hack. “Don’t follow a career path, follow your path. Listen to what your heart is telling you,” he says. “But feeling right has to come from a place of service, not ego. When you act from ego, you optimize for status. When you act from service, you optimize for impact.”

He adds a shorter list underneath that: be yourself, be honest, have fun at work, and don’t try to solve problems alone. “And be fearless,” he says. “Being fearless doesn’t mean never feeling fear. It means refusing to let fear be the deciding factor.”

Staying Grounded While Building

For all the talk of AI and business models, Nils Ehle is unusually candid about what keeps him functional as a founder: going analog. He plays the handpan, runs, does physical work, and spends time in nature with his family. “Those moments aren’t breaks from work, they’re part of how the work happens,” he says. “New ideas rarely arrive when you’re staring at the problem. They arrive when you’ve stepped away.”

He describes his approach to balance less as a goal and more as a practice of letting go. “When you operate from a controlling stance, you live from ego, and you spend enormous energy fighting reality,” Nils Ehle says. “Once you live differently, balance stops being something you achieve. It becomes something you are.”

title: Top 10 Global Leaders Creating Lasting Impact
author: Entrepreneur Mirror
excerpt: There’s a difference between being in charge and actually leading, and most people can tell within minutes which one they’re dealing with. The leaders on this list fall firmly into the second category. They didn’t just occupy positions of influence; they used them to build something that held up long after the initial buzz wore off. A policy that actually worked years later. A company culture that outlived its founder’s tenure. A community program that kept running long after the cameras left. That’s what we’re after here, not the flashiest names, but the ones whose fingerprints are still visible on the world today. This roundup of the top 10 global leaders looks past the headlines to the work that actually held up. Inside the List of Top Leaders Making a Mark This list brings together the top 10 global leaders from different corners of the world, working across sectors as varied as their approaches. A quick look at what they’ve built and why it’s still standing. 1. Merissa Boey | Building a Smarter Way to Discover Technology & Software Solutions “Software and technology solutions should be accessible, transparent, and easy to navigate for businesses of every size.” That belief sits at the heart of everything Merissa Boey is building. A policy that actually worked years later. A company culture that outlived its founder’s tenure. A community program that kept running long after the cameras left. That’s what we’re after here, not the flashiest names, but the ones whose fingerprints are still visible on the world today. This roundup of the top 10 global leaders looks past the headlines to the work that actually held up.

Inside the List of Top Leaders Making a Mark

This list brings together the top 10 global leaders from different corners of the world, working across sectors as varied as their approaches. A quick look at what they’ve built and why it’s still standing.
